items.title: Housing optimism fades as Canadians brace for higher inflation
items.description: Most Canadians expect inflation to climb as the Bank of Canada weighs an October rate hike
items.content: <p>Most Canadians expect inflation to climb as the Bank of Canada weighs an October rate hike</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639269897481153104.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Most Canadians expect inflation to climb as the Bank of Canada weighs an October rate hike
items.body:
Canadians are bracing for higher prices even as their faith in the economy and the housing market fades. That combination complicates the Bank of Canada's next interest rate decision and the conversations mortgage brokers are having with clients.

The Bloomberg Nanos Canadian Confidence Index fell to 50.45 in the four weeks ended Oct. 2, from 51.80 a month earlier, according to Nanos Research.

A reading of 50 marks the line between net optimism and net pessimism, so consumer confidence now sits at roughly neutral. That is well below the index's long-run average of 54.67.

A separate Nanos poll for Bloomberg News, conducted Sept. 27 to 29, found that 54% of Canadians expect annual inflation to be above the current 3% a year from now. Only 7% expect it to ease.

"The result is a public mood marked less by alarm than by caution: households are holding steady, yet doubts about Canada's economic direction continue to cap enthusiasm," Nik Nanos, chief data scientist at Nanos Research, said in the report.

Housing expectations weaken as consumer confidence stalls

The weakness shows up mainly in forward-looking views. The index's expectations gauge tracks sentiment on the economy and real estate prices, and it dropped to 46.75 from 48.76.

Just 28.54% of respondents expect home values in their neighbourhood to rise over the next six months, down from 32.67% four weeks earlier.

Personal finances are holding up better. The pocketbook gauge covers finances and job security, and it slipped only to 54.15 from 54.83.

Still, 39.21% of Canadians said they are worse off than a year ago, compared with 10.60% who feel better off.

Sentiment is weakest in British Columbia, at 44.52. In Ontario, the reading fell to 48.53 from 52.42.

Among renters, confidence dropped to 48.51 from 54.27 over the same four weeks.

Aled ab Iorwerth, deputy chief economist at CMHC, says rising bond yields, inflation concerns, and trade-related uncertainty are making the outlook for interest rates and housing activity increasingly difficult to predict. https://t.co/mkip7w5Cba — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 6, 2026

What do rising inflation expectations mean for a Bank of Canada rate hike?

Inflation expectations matter because they can fulfil themselves. If households build higher prices into wage demands or bring purchases forward, the central bank's job gets harder.

Governor Tiff Macklem has warned that moving slowly carries its own cost. "Two things probably have to happen if you're too slow: One is, you're going to have to raise rates very quickly," he said in a recent speech in Halifax.

The policy rate has held at 2.25% since October 2025. Traders in overnight swaps put the odds of a hike at the Oct. 28 meeting at about one in three. Meanwhile, a growing number of major forecasters now expect an October increase.

Not every forecaster agrees. Helen Lao, an economist at Toronto-based CIBC Capital Markets, argues that Canada's inflation is largely driven by fuel prices. "In Canada, inflation is much less broad-based," she wrote in a report arguing the case for a Canadian hike is weaker than the Fed's.

For brokers, the rate debate comes down to the choice between fixed and variable. A quarter-point hike would flow straight through to the prime rate, now 4.45%.

Leah Zlatkin, a Toronto-based licensed mortgage broker and LowestRates.ca expert, said the gap between fixed and variable pricing is complicating client conversations.

"With variable rates still coming in below comparable fixed rates, I'm seeing more interest from clients who are weighing whether the lower rate is worth the added uncertainty," she said.

The Bank of Canada will publish its quarterly business and consumer surveys on Oct. 19. They will give a fresh read on household inflation expectations nine days before the rate decision.

items.title: Why September's resale slump is spreading across Canadian markets
items.description: RBC Economics says trade tensions and higher long-term rates sidelined buyers in September
items.content: <p>RBC Economics says trade tensions and higher long-term rates sidelined buyers in September</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639269859968708544.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: RBC Economics says trade tensions and higher long-term rates sidelined buyers in September
items.body:
Home resales fell across most of Canada's major housing markets in September, as escalating trade tensions with the United States and rising long-term interest rates pushed buyers back to the sidelines, according to Royal Bank of Canada (RBC) Economics.

In its October housing update, RBC assistant chief economist Robert Hogue reported transaction declines at local real estate boards in Vancouver, the Fraser Valley, Calgary, Edmonton, Winnipeg, Hamilton, Kitchener-Waterloo, Toronto, Ottawa, Montreal and Quebec City.

Among the six largest markets, year-over-year resales dropped by between 4% in Calgary and 12% in Montreal.

The pullback comes just weeks after RBC characterized August's slowdown as a temporary detour rather than a derailment.

"Diverging trends across the country reflect different states of confidence, affordability, pent-up demand, demographics, job markets and market inventory. Even macroeconomic factors like interest rates and immigration policy see their impact shaped by the local context," the report said.

Toronto and Vancouver lead home price declines

Ontario and British Columbia remain the weakest links. In the Vancouver area, the composite MLS Home Price Index (HPI) – a benchmark tracking the value of a typical home – sat 5.5% below year-ago levels.

Resales, meanwhile, fell nearly 8% from August on a seasonally adjusted basis.

"Further depreciation will likely be necessary to draw in more buyers," the report said, warning that with active listings near a decade high, price weakness could last through this year and "possibly into 2027."

Toronto's brief rebound proved short-lived.

"It didn't take long for the tentative recovery to go off course in the Toronto area. The timid rally lasted just five months to August," the report said.

Resales slipped 5.2% month-over-month in September, and the condo price index fell 6.7% year-over-year, versus 4.7% for single-detached homes.

Calgary held relatively steady, with its benchmark price down 0.8% annually, while Montreal's inventory climbed 20% from a year earlier on the strongest influx of sellers in six years.

What does an uneven recovery mean for brokers?

RBC's own data showed housing affordability gains nearly stalled in the second quarter, with the bank warning that "upward pressure on long-term interest rates and likelihood of Bank of Canada hikes next year could put ownership costs on the rise again after dropping significantly since 2024."

Some brokers remain upbeat. Drew Donaldson, principal at Toronto-based Donaldson Capital, told Canadian Mortgage Professional last month he expected activity to hold up despite the bond market turbulence lifting fixed rates.

"The fall market and Q4 is typically a strong finish to the year and we're expecting even with higher rates that it'll remain busy and pick up steam," he said.

RBC also sees eventual improvement, though not a smooth one.

"Generally, we expect improving affordability and a resilient economy will progressively unlock pent-up demand and support a mild recovery in Canada. But, the road ahead is likely to be bumpy and uneven across markets," the report said.

items.title: Canadians trade convenience for space as housing compromise deepens
items.description: REMAX survey finds buyers flexing on location and finances as buyer-favourable conditions spread
items.content: <p>REMAX survey finds buyers flexing on location and finances as buyer-favourable conditions spread</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639269843340385358.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: REMAX survey finds buyers flexing on location and finances as buyer-favourable conditions spread
items.body:
More than six in ten Canadians say they would relocate or restructure their personal finances to afford a better-suited home, according to REMAX Canada's 2026 Fall Housing Market Outlook.

The outlook draws from a Leger survey of 1,532 Canadian adults conducted between July 17 and 19, which found 65% of respondents willing to make at least one compromise on location, property type, or financial structure to access a more suitable home.

Aled ab Iorwerth, deputy chief economist at CMHC, says rising bond yields, inflation concerns, and trade-related uncertainty are making the outlook for interest rates and housing activity increasingly difficult to predict. https://t.co/mkip7w5Cba — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 6, 2026

Where buyers are willing to give ground

Location leads the list of concessions. Nearly two-thirds (63%) said they would relocate for a home that better meets their needs, with 47% willing to move up to an hour away and 16% prepared to go even farther.

An additional 31% would accept greater distance from a city centre, while 21% would trade proximity to shops and other amenities.

Financial trade-offs are just as common. Forty-one% said they would cut discretionary spending, such as travel and dining, to fund a purchase, while 24% would extend their mortgage amortization.

Thirty-year amortizations have given more buyers a path to qualification, though experienced brokers consistently flag the long-term interest cost as a conversation that cannot be skipped.

A further 17% said they would delay retirement savings or take on additional income sources.

Don Kottick, President of REMAX Canada, framed the shift as practical recalibration.

"There's a difference between compromising and settling," he said. "Buyers are identifying what matters most and where they have room to be flexible."

Affordability ranked as the dominant search criterion, cited by 60% of respondents, with neighbourhood safety second at 47%.

A softer market, but buyer conditions improving

REMAX brokers and agents reported that home sales declined year-over-year in 81% of markets analyzed between January 1 and July 31, while average residential prices rose in 56% of markets.

The fall outlook projects 2026 national sales finishing approximately 2% below 2025 levels.

Yet buyer-favourable conditions have spread further than anticipated at the start of the year. REMAX estimates 32% of markets will sit in buyers' territory this fall, compared with 15.2% a year earlier.

"The market has not become easy for buyers, but in many regions, it is allowing for a more deliberate purchasing process," Kottick said.

For mortgage brokers, the data describes a client base that has not stepped away from homeownership, but arrives with recalibrated priorities and a clear willingness to flex on geography, property condition, and amortisation structure.

items.title: Expert: We Must Build A Better Trades Training System (Or Housing Will Continue To Suffer)
items.description:
Canada has finally begun to confront its housing crisis with the urgency that it so rightly deserves.

In Ontario, policy initiatives have signalled a renewed commitment to getting more homes built. Federally, there is growing recognition that increasing supply is essential to restoring affordability.

These efforts deserve praise. Policymakers have acknowledged the scale of the challenge and taken meaningful steps to address it. But there’s another reality we can’t ignore. None of these housing ambitions will be achieved unless we have the skilled workforce needed to build them.

Every housing target ultimately depends on the availability of carpenters, electricians, plumbers, bricklayers, heavy equipment operators and dozens of other skilled tradespeople. Without them, housing policies become little more than plans on paper.

That is why the findings of the recent report Are We Ready to Build Canada? A Behavioural Analysis of Canada’s Construction Talent Pipeline and Skills Training Policy should serve as a wake-up call.

The report was prepared for RESCON by Nathaniel Barr, professor of creativity and senior advisor, innovation at Sheridan College; Michael McNamara, professor of creativity and director of the Community Ideas Factory at Sheridan; and James K. Stewart, economist and a senior fellow at the C.D. Howe Institute.

The report argues that Canada's apprenticeship challenge is not primarily an economic problem. It is a design problem.

That conclusion may seem surprising at first. For years, governments have responded to labour shortages by increasing funding, promoting careers in the skilled trades and creating programs designed to attract more apprentices. Those efforts have succeeded in one important respect: registrations have increased.

The problem is that completions have not.

The report highlights a startling statistic. Apprenticeship completion rates in Canada have remained stuck at roughly 20% of registrations since 2013. In other words, four out of five people who begin the apprenticeship journey are not completing it within the current system.

Imagine a university where only one in five students graduated. Policymakers would rightly view that as a crisis requiring immediate attention. Yet in the skilled trades, this troubling reality has persisted for more than a decade.

The implications extend far beyond the apprenticeship system itself. Every apprentice who fails to complete training represents a lost opportunity to strengthen Canada's workforce. Fewer certified tradespeople mean fewer homes built, longer infrastructure timelines and reduced economic productivity.

The urgency is magnified by demographics. More than 700,000 skilled trades workers are expected to retire by 2028. In construction alone, approximately 15% of the workforce is projected to retire by 2034.

While the labour market has temporarily eased workforce pressures, policymakers should not be lulled into complacency. Many workers have already left the residential construction industry because of current market conditions. When housing demand rebounds and construction activity accelerates, the industry could find itself confronting severe labour shortages.

The traditional approach has focused heavily on recruitment. The assumption has been that if enough people enter apprenticeship programs, completion rates will take care of themselves.

But the report challenges that thinking.

Drawing on behavioural science, the authors maintain that apprenticeship systems have been designed around unrealistic assumptions about how people make decisions and navigate challenges. Policymakers have often assumed that individuals will act rationally, remain motivated, overcome obstacles independently and persist until completion.

Human behaviour rarely works that way.

People face competing demands from work and family. They become overwhelmed by complexity. They struggle with uncertainty and self-doubt. They procrastinate. They abandon plans when obstacles appear insurmountable. These are not character flaws. They are normal aspects of human behaviour.

Behavioural science examines those realities and seeks to design systems that account for them.

That insight has profound implications for apprenticeship policy.

If apprentices are struggling because application processes are unnecessarily complicated, simplify them. If critical stages of training create bottlenecks, provide targeted supports. If participants lose momentum during long training periods, develop interventions that maintain engagement. If social isolation contributes to attrition, create mentoring programs that strengthen connections and accountability.

In short, we need apprenticeship systems designed around how people actually behave, not how policymakers wish they behaved.

This does not mean funding is unimportant. Continued investments in apprenticeship programs, labour market information forecasting and skills training remain essential. And governments should continue supporting efforts to attract young Canadians into the skilled trades.

But funding alone will not solve a problem rooted in system design.

Governments need to make apprenticeship completion rates a central performance measure. Success should not be defined by how many people enter the system. It should be defined by how many emerge as certified tradespeople.

The country is about to embark on one of the most ambitious building agendas in generations. Our ability to build more homes depends on our ability to train, support and retain more skilled tradespeople.

If we want to build more homes, we must first build a better system for the people who build them.

Richard Lyall is president of the Residential Construction Council of Ontario (RESCON). He has represented the building industry in Ontario since 1991. Contact him at media@rescon.com.

items.title: Bryan Yu: B.C. housing starts rebound in August despite weak construction outlook
items.description: Weak presales, excess inventory and a slowing construction pipeline point to softer activity ahead in B.C.
items._ogDesc: Weak presales, excess inventory and a slowing construction pipeline point to softer activity ahead in B.C.
items.body:
Housing starts in B.C. jumped in August, but the increase does not indicate strength in the construction cycle as new projects remain paused due to poor market conditions, excess inventory and saturated rental markets.

Urban B.C. housing starts rose by 39 per cent to a seasonally adjusted annualized rate of 39,715 units, following three consecutive monthly declines. The increase was driven by a 44.6 per cent jump in multi-family starts, while single-family starts declined 1.7 per cent.

However, housing starts fluctuate from month-to-month, and the six-month moving average remained subdued. On a year-over-year basis, housing starts in urban centres fell 7.6 per cent and were down 9.7 per cent year-to-date. Both multi-family and single-family starts declined at a comparable pace during the first eight months of the year.

Within multi-family housing, the year-to-date decline was driven by a 13.6 per cent decrease in apartment starts, which account for most new housing construction in the province. In contrast, semi-detached and row housing starts increased 30.4 per cent and 0.8 per cent, respectively.

Among B.C.'s major urban markets, year-to-date, starts declined in Abbotsford-Mission (-47.7 per cent), Kelowna (-35.5 per cent), Vancouver (-6 per cent), and Victoria (-40.8 per cent). In contrast, starts increased by 41.7 per cent in Chilliwack and by 70.3 per cent in Nanaimo, while starts in Kamloops more than doubled compared with the same period last year.

Despite weaker starts, more than 84,000 units remain under construction across B.C., primarily apartments in Vancouver, reflecting earlier construction decisions and long project completion timelines. Low pre-sale sell-through and weak residential building permit activity signal slower construction ahead, raising concerns about future housing supply and affordability.

On the employment front, business-reported payroll counts in B.C. were essentially unchanged in July, edging down by 514 positions, or less than 0.1 per cent, to approximately 2.59 million. This followed a similarly modest decline of 329 positions in June. Payroll employment remained 0.7 per cent, or 19,962 positions, above its year-earlier level. Nevertheless, the recent monthly weakness points to subdued employment growth.

Excluding unclassified businesses, payroll employment declined by 1,304 positions. This measure provides the basis for the industry breakdown below. By comparison, the Labour Force Survey reported a monthly employment increase of 17,800 in July, although the two surveys measure employment differently.

Goods-producing industries lost 554 payroll positions in July, leaving employment 0.6 per cent, or 2,124 positions, below its year-earlier level at approximately 388,990.

Manufacturing posted the largest monthly decline, shedding 754 positions, and was down 1,213 positions from a year earlier. Construction employment fell by 568 positions during the month and by 436 year-over- year. In contrast, utilities added 554 positions in July and 1,090 positions over the previous 12 months.

Service-producing payroll employment declined by 750 positions in July but remained 1.3 per cent, or 29,118 positions, above its year-earlier level.

Accommodation and food services led the monthly gains, adding 870 positions and recording a fourth consecutive increase. Administrative and support, waste management and remediation services added 660 positions, reversing the previous month’s decline. Educational services recorded the largest monthly decrease, losing 803 positions, while health care and social assistance declined by 800 positions. Despite these monthly declines, health care and social assistance posted the largest year-over-year gain, at 10,376 positions, followed by educational services at 7,486 positions.

Average weekly earnings rose 0.6 per cent in July and by 4.5 per cent from a year earlier, reaching $1,356.78. The increase was robust but partly reflected the composition of hiring. The job vacancy rate remained at 3.1 per cent for a third consecutive month, corresponding to approximately 79,585 vacant positions.

Bryan Yu is chief economist at Central 1.

items.body:
Greater Toronto’s real estate recovery experienced another setback last month. Toronto Regional Real Estate Board (TRREB) data shows home sales pulled back in September. Falling sales met with historically lofty inventory, helping to push home prices to a 6-year low.

Toronto Home Prices Fall To 6-Year Low

The composite benchmark price of a home across TRREB.

Source: TRREB; CREA; Better Dwelling.

The price of a typical home slipped 0.9% (-$8.3k) to $917,600 in September, down 4.7% (-$45.2k) from last year. Last month marked the fourth consecutive month of declines and pushed prices 28.3% (-$362.2k) below the March 2022 peak. A typical home across Greater Toronto is now back to September 2020 levels—a 6 year low.

Toronto Sees Fewer Sales, Inventory Remains Historically High

Greater Toronto home sales vs active listings of homes for sales in September.

Source: TRREB; CREA; Better Dwelling.

Sales continue to slide as the recovery hits a bump. TRREB reported 5,040 sales in September, 9.0% lower than last year and the weakest volume for the month since 2023. That said, it was still the second-weakest September in over 15 years of data.

Inventory is starting to firm, though it remains historically elevated for the demand level. There were 16,500 new listings in September, 14.4% lower than last year. On its own, this volume would be consistent with historical volumes around this time of year. In the context of current demand, it’s a lot—leaving the sales-to-new listings ratio (SNLR) at 30%, where prices are expected to fall even further.

One of the reasons for the slide in new listings might be just how much inventory is kicking around. There were 26,131 active listings in September, 9.3% below last year. However, the number is still the second-most for the month going back to at least 2010. Once again, another problem amplified by demand falling to one of its weakest levels on record.

items.title: Metro Vancouver office construction falls to lowest level in 15 years
items.description: Softer office demand has prompted some proposed projects to shift toward alternative uses or remain on hold: Cushman & Wakefield
items._ogDesc: Softer office demand has prompted some proposed projects to shift toward alternative uses or remain on hold: Cushman & Wakefield
items.body:
Metro Vancouver’s office construction pipeline declined to 1.12 million square feet in the third quarter, the lowest level since 2011, according to new research from commercial real estate firm Cushman & Wakefield.

The decline comes as Metro Vancouver’s office vacancy rate climbed to its highest level since the early 2000s, driven largely by several significant tenant move-outs and technology-sector consolidation, particularly in the downtown core.

“Softer office demand has prompted some proposed projects to shift toward alternative uses, reducing the future office development pipeline to approximately 7.6 million square feet,” said Cushman & Wakefield in a Monday news release.

“Several proposed developments remain on hold as developers await stronger demand and sufficient pre-leasing before beginning construction.”

Fourteen office projects are currently under construction across the region, with about 49 per cent of the space already pre-leased or pre-sold. The largest concentrations of new inventory are in the Broadway corridor, Burnaby, False Creek and New Westminster, according to the firm.

About 138,000 square feet of new office space was delivered during the third quarter, while another 274,000 square feet is scheduled for completion through year-end. This puts 2026 deliveries on pace to total about 548,000 square feet, the lowest annual level since 2021, Cushman & Wakefield said.

“The significant pullback in development is becoming an increasingly important part of the outlook,” said Svetlana Lebedeva, research manager at Cushman & Wakefield.

“Even with demand remaining selective today, very little new supply is moving forward. As existing options are absorbed, that could create tighter conditions for tenants seeking larger, high-quality blocks, particularly on higher floors, over the longer term.”

Sublease vacancy declined for the 12th consecutive quarter, with sublease space accounting for 13.6 per cent of total vacant inventory in the third quarter, down from 13.9 per cent in the second quarter and about 22 per cent a year earlier. 

Despite the high overall vacancy, large contiguous options "remain limited" in the region, with 10 blocks larger than 60,000 square feet currently available across Metro Vancouver, Cushman & Wakefield said.

While fewer large new tenants are entering the market, several significant renewals during the quarter showed "continued demand" from existing occupiers, according to Cushman & Wakefield. Demand has increasingly shifted toward the region’s traditional office occupiers, including government, financial services, engineering, mining and energy companies, as the influx of large U.S. technology companies has subsided, the company added.

“Metro Vancouver’s headline vacancy rate doesn’t tell the full story of the market,” Lebedeva said.

“We continue to see tenants take a more measured approach to space decisions, but large blocks remain relatively scarce, sublease inventory continues to decline and the development pipeline has contracted considerably. Those dynamics are creating a much more nuanced environment than the overall vacancy number would suggest.”

items.title: KingSett Capital Lists Two King Street East Office Towers In Downtown Toronto
items.description:
Two high-profile high-rise office towers in downtown Toronto have officially hit the market, according to a new listing that came online last week.

The first tower is 8 King Street East, a 21-storey office tower located at the northeast corner of Yonge Street and King Street East. The building was originally constructed in 1915, and is home to 155,888 sq. ft of net leasable area, 92% of which is leased with a weighted average lease term of 3.5 years.

The second tower is 18 King Street East, an 18-storey office tower located at the northwest corner of the intersection of King Street East and Victoria Street. The building was originally constructed in 1968 and is home to 238,746 sq. ft of net leasable area, 100% of which is leased with a weighted average lease term of 5.3 years.

The two Class B office buildings sit on the same block in the financial district and are separated by the narrow office building at 10 King Street East. The location provides convenient access to King Station, Union Station, as well as the PATH network.

8 and 18 King Street East in Toronto. (RBC Capital Markets Realty)

Combined, 8 and 18 King Street East total to 394,634 sq. ft of net leasable space — including some ground-level retail space — that is 96.8% leased to 88 tenants with an overall weighted average lease term of 4.6 years.

The properties are owned by private equity real estate investment firm KingSett Capital — through KingSett Real Estate Growth LP No. 6 — and KingSett has achieved those numbers by completing over 35 lease transactions — new leases and lease renewals — within the past 12 months, according to the listing.

The Listing

8 and 18 King Street East were both listed on an unpriced basis last week by David Tweedie, Tim Pacaud, and Keith Chan of RBC Capital Markets Realty, which called it “a rare opportunity to acquire two well-located assets of scale within a market defined by tightening supply and accelerating demand for quality office space.”

The two buildings are being made available either separately or together. Notably, however, 8 King Street East is being offered on a freehold basis, while 18 King Street East is being offered on a leasehold basis, according to the listing brochure.

  • Address: 8 King Street East / 18 King Street East
  • Year Built: 1915 / 1968
  • Site Area: 0.22 acre / 0.49 acre
  • Gross Leasable Area: 155,888 sq. ft / 238,746 sq. ft
  • Current Occupancy Rate: 92% / 100% (Blended 96.8%)
  • Price: Unpriced
  • Listed By: RBC Capital Markets Realty (David Tweedie, Tim Pacaud, Keith Chan)

“Designed by Ross and Macdonald and constructed in 1915 as the global headquarters of the Royal Bank of Canada, 8 King is among Toronto’s most architecturally significant office properties,” said RBC in its brochure. “The Vendor completed a comprehensive exterior rehabilitation at 8 King in 2021, earning the Peter Stokes Restoration Award for best practice in heritage conservation.”

Interior photos of 8 and 18 King Street East. (RBC Capital Markets Realty)

“Across the Properties, the Vendor has invested over $20MM in capital improvements since 2014, including lobby modernization, elevator recommissioning, underground garage rehabilitation at 18 King, and ongoing mechanical and roofing programs — evidencing active and disciplined asset stewardship.”

According to RBC, downtown Toronto’s office market continues to show improvement. The downtown vacancy rate is now down to 13.6% as of Q2 2026, which represents the lowest level since Q4 2022. Specific to the financial district, the vacancy rate is even lower — 11.9%.

Year-to-date net absorption of office space in the Greater Toronto Area totalled to 2.7 million sq. ft in the first half of 2026, which RBC says is the strongest first-half performance in years. Accordingly, “A sharply depleted new supply pipeline in H2 2026 reinforces the structural advantage of well-located assets such as the Properties and sets the stage for continued vacancy compression in Toronto's Financial Core.”

items.title: Two Thirds Of GTA Condos Sold For Less Than $600K In September
items.description:
Of the 1,316 condominium apartments sold across the GTA in September, 893 sold for less than $600,000. Nearly half, 594 units, sold below $500,000.

That puts 67.9% of condo sales below $600,000 and 45.1% below half a million. For buyers trying to work out whether ownership is within reach, those transactions offer a more useful starting point than the GTA's $1,006,409 average price across all housing types.

The largest single condo price band was $400,000 to $499,999, with 390 sales. Another 299 apartments sold between $500,000 and $599,999.

The table cannot tell a buyer whether a suitable two-bedroom apartment is available at that price in a particular neighbourhood. It covers the units that sold, with no adjustment for their size or location.

Prices fell faster than in the other major categories

The average condo apartment sold for $605,257 in September, down 7.7% from a year earlier, according to the Toronto Regional Real Estate Board's Market Watch report. That was the largest average-price decline among the four major housing categories in its summary table.

Detached prices fell 5.1%, the combined townhouse category fell 4.6%, and semi-detached prices were down 0.2%.

These are changes in the averages of homes sold, so shifts in the mix of properties affect the result. They do not mean every condo lost 7.7% of its value.

Condo sales totalled 1,316, down 7.8% from September 2025. Across all housing types, GTA sales fell 9% to 5,040. The weakness extended beyond apartments, but the condo market paired falling transactions with the steepest average-price decline in that four-category comparison.

The price decline was larger outside Toronto

The City of Toronto's average condo selling price was $640,248, down 6.1% from a year earlier. In TRREB's 905 category, which covers its reporting area outside the City of Toronto, it was $533,654, down 12%.

The $106,594 gap gives a buyer willing to change location a reason to compare apartments beyond Toronto's boundary. It is a difference between the units sold in the two areas; it does not measure the saving from moving an otherwise identical apartment into the suburbs.

A lower purchase price also needs to be weighed against condominium fees and the building's finances. The report supplies selling prices, leaving the buyer to examine the obligations attached to each unit.

The cheaper 905 average coincided with a larger decline in sales. Toronto recorded 884 condo transactions, down 5.5% year-over-year. The 905 recorded 432, down 12.4%. Both areas offered lower average prices than a year earlier; neither recorded more sales.

The sales figures cannot establish why households held back. A developer counting on lower prices to lift transactions would need to look beyond September's result.

New condos have plenty of resale competition

At the end of September, 8,226 condo apartments were listed for sale across TRREB's coverage area. Of those, 5,329 were in Toronto and 2,897 were in the 905.

Dividing those month-end listings by September's sales produces ratios of 6.0 in Toronto and 6.7 in the 905. Each area had roughly six or seven apartments listed at month-end for every apartment sold during September.

Properties arrive on the market and listings expire throughout the month, so this calculation compares available stock with one month's transactions. It differs from TRREB's published inventory trend measure and cannot forecast how long a particular unit will take to sell. Buyers have a selection of existing apartments to compare before committing.

For a new condominium project, those existing apartments are part of the competition. A prospective purchaser can compare the proposed unit's price and features with nearby resales. Any premium needs a reason that matters to that purchaser, such as a better layout or a location closer to work.

September's regional price bands do not set the correct price for a new unit. A small apartment in an older building is a poor comparable for a larger unit in a different neighbourhood. The bands do show where most completed condo purchases landed, which makes them a useful check on assumptions about the budgets a project will serve.

That check needs to include the total price. A unit can look competitive on a price-per-square-foot basis and still require a budget beyond what its intended purchaser can spend. Market Watch's price-band table does not include floor area, so it cannot resolve that comparison. It shows the total prices buyers agreed to pay.

Market Watch measures resales. It does not measure condo presales, construction starts, completions or developer finances. Those require their own evidence. A new project's price has to hold up against the resale units its target purchaser can afford today.

items.title: Metro Vancouver leads North America in new luxury store openings
items.description: The luxury surge comes as Vancouver’s broader retail market remains constrained by a lack of new supply: JLL
items._ogDesc: The luxury surge comes as Vancouver’s broader retail market remains constrained by a lack of new supply: JLL
items.body:
Metro Vancouver has emerged as North America’s leading market for new luxury store openings, fuelled by the spring 2026 opening of Oakridge Park, according to a recent report from commercial real estate firm JLL.

The Vancouver market recorded 30 new luxury openings between July 2025 and July 2026, putting it ahead of New York City, which had 18, and some other traditional luxury retail hubs including Miami and Los Angeles, according to JLL’s Canada retail market dynamics report released last week.

“The opening of Oakridge Park … has pushed luxury to 43 per cent of Canadian new fashion openings this year and surprisingly placed Vancouver ahead of New York City in luxury openings,” according to the report.

The opening of Oakridge Park has made Vancouver one of Canada’s most significant luxury retail clusters and Western Canada’s counterpart to Toronto’s Yorkdale and Montréal’s Royalmount, according to JLL.

However, the luxury boom comes as Vancouver’s broader retail market remains constrained by a lack of new supply.

Retail vacancy in Metro Vancouver stood at 2.6 per cent in the first half of 2026, down 0.1 percentage points from the end of 2025 and 1.4 percentage points above levels before the Hudson’s Bay closures.

Downtown Vancouver’s retail vacancy rate was 9.9 per cent during this period, while Surrey and Langley saw some of the lowest rates in Canada at 1.5 per cent in each market.

“The underlying picture is more nuanced: leasing activity is declining, rent growth is decelerating, and retail sales growth is slowing as trade uncertainty and food inflation continue to weigh on non-essential retail,” the report said.

The region’s mall vacancy declined from a 6.5 per cent peak to 6.1 per cent, but leasing activity declined six per cent from the first half of 2025.

JLL said the lack of supply explains much of the leasing activity decline, noting that the amount of retail space under construction fell “sharply” to 526,000 square feet following the completion of Oakridge Park, with construction starts near decade lows.

“With Vancouver’s pipeline concentrated in transit-oriented mixed-use redevelopment, the market has no mechanism to add meaningful new inventory in the near term,” the report said.

JLL expects Vancouver’s retail market to strengthen as population growth resumes in 2027, while improving consumer spending and tourism support demand.

The Broadway corridor, under construction for the Millennium Line extention, is one of the most compelling retail repositioning opportunities in the region, the report added.

“The underlying conditions that make Vancouver one of Canada's most supply-constrained retail markets continue to strengthen, with the supply pipeline near decade lows,” the report said.

“The structural conditions for the next tightening cycle—scarce land, affluent demographics, international brand demand, and a freshly repositioned luxury tier—are arguably stronger in Vancouver than anywhere else in Canada.”

Vancouver’s average asking retail rent reached $39.44 per square foot in the first half of 2026, the highest among the major Canadian markets tracked by JLL. Rents increased 3.3 per cent year over year, down from a 5.4 per cent peak in 2024, according to JLL.

items.body:
Canadians just made the largest migration across provinces in 3 years. Statistics Canada (StatCan) data shows 116,832 residents in Q2 2026 made an interprovincial migration, the most since 2023. The numbers reveal Alberta continues to be the top spot in the country for people looking for a new province. Meanwhile in Ontario, the mass exodus continues as residents seek better opportunities.

Alberta and BC Continue To Attract Canadians, Ontario Not So Much

Canadian interprovincial migration by province: the balance of residents that left for another province and those who arrived, Q2 2026.

Source: StatCan; Better Dwelling.

Canadians continue to flock to Alberta, with the biggest net positive inflow in the country. The province managed to score 5,893 more residents from other provinces than it lost in Q2. It was followed by British Columbia (B.C.) with a net gain of 2,756 in the quarter. In a distant third place was Nova Scotia with a net gain of 963 residents from other provinces.

Ontario continues to hemorrhage residents with a net loss of 7,063 residents in Q2. It was followed by Manitoba (-1,847) and Quebec (-1,233). The agency’s numbers don’t tell us why or who exactly is moving in this flow, but the rapid climb in housing costs in these provinces is likely a contributor. However, B.C.’s wins are a kink in that narrative.

Alberta Leads As Top Destination From Other Provinces By A Wide Margin, Ontario’s Problems Look Structural

Canadian interprovincial migration by province: the balance of residents that left for another province and those who arrived, rolling 12-month sum Q2 2026.

Source: StatCan; Better Dwelling.

Over the past year, Alberta has taken the crown as the undisputed top destination for Canadians. The province saw a net gain of 26,376 residents from other provinces, as it focuses on fostering domestic talent. In a distant second is Nova Scotia (+7,315), which has been punching above its weight in recent years. However, its net gain in Q2 2026 was roughly 47.2% lower than last year, pointing to a sharp deceleration as outflows rise and inflows slow. New Brunswick (+5,121) rounds out the top 3 for the largest net gains over the 12-month period.

Ontario remains the undisputed champion when it comes to losses, with a net loss of 29,713 residents to other provinces. The problem is starting to look structural, as it prioritizes immigration-based growth instead of domestic retention. For context, that loss is more than 3x the net outflows in Quebec (-8,058) and 9x that of Manitoba (-3,175) over the same period. That’s not a quarterly blip, it should be considered a hair-on-fire problem.

These losses aren’t just a shuffle, these are residents familiar with what a province has to offer—or not. It’s a window into the state of the region and the opportunities it presents. Policymakers are unlikely to notice the losses over the short-term, as immigration more than covers the headline outflows. But it’s not as easy as it may seem to fill the talent gap over the medium term—or retain the highest quality immigrants, who are also likely to flow where the opportunity is presented.

items.title: Toronto Rolls Out Free Pre-Approved Plans For Fourplexes, Sixplexes
items.description:
Toronto property owners looking to add homes to their lots can now start from a set of drawings the City is offering for free.

The City has announced four multiplex designs for its Pre-Approved Building Plans Program, which already offered plans for garden and laneway suites. The new plans include two fourplexes and two sixplexes, each drawn for either a narrow or a wide lot.

LGA Architectural Partners won the City's RFP to design them, with accessibility, climate resilience, cost and ease of construction among the stated priorities.

According to the City, the program lines up with Toronto's expanded multiplex zoning permissions. A fourplex is allowed anywhere in the city today, while sixplex permissions depend on where the property is located. An owner whose multiplex fits the zoning rules can go straight to a building permit application, with no stop at the Committee of Adjustment.

The pre-approval covers the building as designed. The City has confirmed each one meets the Ontario Building Code and the zoning rules that govern its design. Where it sits on a particular lot, and anything else specific to that site, will be reviewed on submission of the permit application.

Narrow Fourplex (City of Toronto)

Wide Sixplex - Side View (City of Toronto)

In terms of process, owners aren't required to submit the pre-approved drawing to get things rolling — they should enter the plan number on the Application to Construct or Demolish form, and reference their chosen HVAC type in the application; the fourplexes come in electric, gas and hybrid versions, and the sixplexes in electric and hybrid.

Site-specific work — mechanical, HVAC and plumbing, and architectural and structural components — falls to qualified design professionals, details of which the City will require in writing. Any modification, including to HVAC or plumbing, voids the plan's pre-approved status, and the owner can apply through the City's regular permit process instead.

The plans can be downloaded at toronto.ca/PreApprovedPlans.

items.title: Intracorp Homes seeks second townhouse project in Shaughnessy
items.description: Developer also wants to build 27 townhouses in the 3700-block of Granville Street
items._ogDesc: Developer also wants to build 27 townhouses in the 3700-block of Granville Street
items.body:
A developer with plans to build 27 townhouses in Shaughnessy has filed another rezoning application with the City of Vancouver to build a similar-sized townhouse project in the same district dominated by single-family homes.

Intracorp Homes’ proposal is for an additional 27 townhouses and the conversion of a heritage house on the property at 1053-1069 Douglas Cres. into a triplex, according to the developer’s rezoning application booklet.

Spread over a 45,209-square-foot site in the “First Shaughnessy” section of the Shaughnessy district, the property consists of two adjacent lots fronting Douglas Crescent. The neighbourhood is almost entirely made up of large single-family homes.

Intracorp had earlier filed a rezoning application with the city to redevelop property in the 3700-block of Granville Street in Shaughnessy to build 27 townhouses. That application calls for the conversion of a protected 1911-era heritage house into a triplex.

Both applications have yet to secure public hearing dates, although the question-and-answer period for staff through the “Shape Your City” website begins Nov. 25 for both proposals.

'Interest in pursuing retention projects'

Intracorp says both projects are centred on the conservation of the heritage houses on the properties—the Capenhurst Residence on Granville and the 1912-era McMillan Residence on Douglas Crescent near Oak Street.

In 2016, the city introduced optional zoning incentives for projects that choose to retain a character house and add strata units and floor area. The projects include renovations to allow multiple units in pre-1940 character homes and/or infill buildings at the rear of a site.

Intracorp says in its rezoning application booklet that an average of 30 character-house retention projects have been filed with the city since 2018. In 2024, there were 25 applications.

“The modest amount of character-retention projects as compared to new construction is largely due to the complexities associated with retaining and converting pre-1940 homes into multi-unit housing and bringing homes up to code for occupant safety and accessibility,” the developer’s booklet said.

“Despite these challenges, some builders and designers continue to be specialists in this type of project and have an interest in pursuing retention projects.”

The McMillan Residence is a 1912 Edwardian-era Foursquare dwelling within Shaughnessy, reflecting the early estate-based development of the neighbourhood.

“Its symmetrical massing, proportions and material expression exemplify the district’s early architectural character,” said the booklet, noting the residence is associated with William and Laura McMillan and later Canadian Pacific Railway executives.

Small-scale, multi-family development

As with its proposal for the 3700-block of Granville Street, Intracorp’s application booklet outlines provincial and municipal government policies designed to open up neighbourhoods for small-scale, multi-family development.

“The proposal delivers a balanced public outcome by aligning multiple policy objectives into a single coherent framework,” the booklet said.

“It secures permanent heritage protection and investment in a significant historic asset, introduces a meaningful supply of family-oriented, ground-oriented housing in a historically low-density area and supports gentle, context-sensitive intensification with a transit-accessible neighbourhood.”

Both applications will be decided by a new city council.

The civic election is Oct. 17, with inauguration day in the first week of November.

items.body:
Time for your cheat sheet on this week’s top stories.

Canadian Real Estate

Canadian Home Prices Back To 2016 Levels After Inflation, Still Out of Reach

Canadian home prices rose—just not in real (inflation-adjusted) terms. BIS data shows home prices in Canada rose 0.78% in Q2 2026, the first increase in a year—though they remain 19.5% below peak. When adjusted to real terms, they slipped again and have fallen nearly 30% since the peak. Home prices are back to 2016 levels after inflation, but affordability isn’t.

Canadian Rents Surged 20%, But the BoC Can’t Explain How It Started

A new Bank of Canada (BoC) study shows asking rents surged over 20% between Q4 2021 and Q4 2026. The researcher shows that population growth and financing explain most growth over the period. What remains a mystery is the year-over-year surge in rents in early 2020, before the pandemic. Most of this growth is “unexplained,” according to the report. This leaves the question: Did a speculative rental bubble drive policymakers to adopt aggressive population growth?

Canada’s International Student Drop Offset By Domestic Surge

Domestic postsecondary enrollment surged in Canada, offsetting declines in foreign students. StatCan data shows total postsecondary enrollment grew 0.14% (+3.2k) to a record 2.35 million in the 2024/25 school year. A breakdown shows international students fell 6.9% (-39.6k) after the recent policy changes. However, domestic enrollment saw growth hit a 14-year high, offsetting the drop.

Canadian GDP Stalls, But Revisions Add 1 In 10 Dollars of 2026 Growth

Canadian GDP was flat in July, but the economy got bigger anyway after revisions. StatCan revisions added 0.1% more than reported growth in 2026. The revision is within the agency’s normal tolerance range, and only worth mentioning due to the slow recent growth reported. The revisions represent roughly 1 in 10 dollars added to GDP year to date.

Canadian Mortgage Arrears Have Skyrocketed 96% As Bank Portfolios Shrink

Canadian banks continue to see mortgage borrowers fall behind on payments. Mortgages in arrears hit 0.29% in July, up 6 basis points in a year and the highest level since May 2014. At the same time, banks saw the number of mortgages on their books fall to 4.91 million in July, marking a 6-year low. Credit use is rising, fewer accounts are driving the growth, and more are buckling under the loads.

items.body:
TORONTO — Store owners might be having a harder time finding rental properties as the amount of retail space under construction in major Canadian markets dropped to its lowest level in a decade.

Retail construction starts amounted to 1.5 million square feet in the first half of this year, commercial real estate firm JLL said in a new report.

That was down from 2.7 million square feet a year prior and 5.3 million square feet in the first half of 2016.

The previous low during the decade came in 2023, when retail construction starts totalled 1.9 million square feet.

JLL's senior vice-president of retail Paul Ferreira attributed the drop in starts to rising building costs, the increasing redevelopment of existing retail space, particularly in malls, and the cancellation of some residential projects that would have had stores on the ground floor.

Ferreira said these factors have left some businesses with fewer rental options.

"Retailers that want to grow are finding it more challenging today to find space than they would have five or 10 years ago," he said Friday. "It means that they have to adapt their formats to the kind of space that is becoming available."

Adding to the challenge are low vacancy rates across most categories of retail space.

Leasing has also declined, the company said.

That's because "first and foremost, there isn't space to move into or some of the larger blocks of space that are available have more homework to be done," Ferreira said.

"Supply is tough to deliver ... so I think landlords who do have the supply are being much more careful in how they are merchandising the space they have and making their long-term decisions."

Many of them have their eye on supermarkets, he said. On the heels of the COVID-19 pandemic, grocers are seen as more stable tenants because they didn't have to temporarily close like other businesses when the economy shut down.

They also drive weekly visits from customers and because they sell essential items, are resilient in the face of inflation and other economic swings.

Plus, other tenants like pharmacies, banks and businesses providing personal services always like to be near a grocer, helping landlords with vacancies, Ferreira said.

JLL's research found that 96 per cent of new properties built since 2022 in what it calls the "daily needs" category are being anchored by grocery tenants, up from 74 per cent between 2016 and 2021.

Grocers had the third highest number of new opening announcements in the first half of this year.

Supermarkets trailed dining establishments, which made up 33 per cent of the opening announcements, and apparel and accessories retailers, which sat at 26 per cent, in JLL's analysis.

Ferreira suspects restaurants are dominating openings because there's still an appetite to dine out after the COVID-19 pandemic and because people are being lured in by new concepts and brands that have moved into major Canadian markets.

"We've seen a lot of growth in quick-service restaurants and fast casual restaurants ... but I don't know how sustainable continued growth in those sectors are," he said.

"As the consumer gets challenged for how much they can eat out of home, I think we'll start to see the market respond to that."

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 2, 2026.

Tara Deschamps, The Canadian Press

items.body:
Canada’s major international student shift hit schools hard, but not enrollment totals. Postsecondary enrollment hit a new high in 2024/2025, according to Statistics Canada (StatCan) data. International enrollment made its sharpest drop in over 30 years, as widely expected. However, a surge in domestic enrollment almost entirely offset the drop.

Canadian Postsecondary Enrollment Growth Is Slow, But Still Growing

Canadian postsecondary enrollment.

Source: StatCan; Better Dwelling.

Canadian post-secondary enrollment hit a new record high of 2.35 million in 2024/2025, up 0.14% (+3.2k) from a year prior. This marks the slowest growth in 5 years, but it follows the sharpest uptick in 20 years—a 5.8% climb in the 2023 school year. For context, the growth in 2023 was so large that it accounts for 3 in 4 students added since the pandemic.

Enrollment growth is a little surprising considering the media blitz on cutbacks. However, breaking this data down by domestic and international enrollment provides some context.

Canada’s International Student Enrollment Just Made Its Sharpest Drop On Record

Annual growth rate for international student enrollment at Canadian postsecondary schools.

Source: StatCan; Better Dwelling.

International enrollment fell to 533,380 in 2024/2025, down 6.9% (-39.59k)—the sharpest drop in the agency’s data. Falling international enrollment is rare, with 2020/2021 being the only other in 25 years. Before that, there was a blip in the mid-90s, during Canada’s last major housing bubble.

Even with the historic drop, international enrollment remains 37.1% higher than pre-pandemic. The drop was largely in Ontario, which accounted for roughly 92% of the net declines.

Lost in the news has been a bright spot—domestic enrollment is making an aggressive climb.

Canada’s Domestic Postsecondary Enrollment Growth Hits A 14-Year High

Annual growth rate for domestic enrollment at Canadian postsecondary schools.

Source: StatCan; Better Dwelling.

Domestic enrollment hit 1.80 million in 2024/2025, up 2.1% (+37.6k) from a year prior. This was the highest enrollment for the segment since 2017 and a 14-year high for growth. The most surprising part? The surge was almost enough to offset the entire international decline.

There’s no immediate explanation for the abrupt climb, but it’s certainly a surprise. It was enough to almost eliminate the policy-driven drop. The data changes the narrative around the “hard hit” colleges.

The post-policy pain reflects a dependence on international enrollment growth, even as the total pushes to a new record high. Ontario’s disproportionate hit also follows a broader trend—young adults are leaving in droves.

items.body:
VANCOUVER — Home sales in the Vancouver region were 8.4 per cent lower last month compared with a year ago, as fewer apartment-style homes changed hands.

Greater Vancouver Realtors says there were 1,717 home sales in September, which was 25 per cent below the 10-year seasonal average.

Andrew Lis, the board's chief economist and vice-president of data analytics, says despite the overall decrease, attached and detached home sales were slightly above last year's levels.

The composite benchmark price for all types of residential properties in Vancouver was $1,075,900, a 5.5 per cent decrease from September 2025 and down 0.6 per cent from August 2026.

There were 5,852 new listings on the market last month, down 10.3 per cent year-over-year but 5.7 per cent above the 10-year average.

Meanwhile, total inventory fell four per cent year-over-year to 16,394, which was 24.3 per cent above the long-term average.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 2, 2026.

items.title: Surrey, SFU Submit Application For New SFU Med School Designed By Stantec, Revery
items.description:
The Surrey City Development Corporation (SCDC) and Simon Fraser University (SFU) have submitted their development permit application for Phase One of Centre Block, which will be home to SFU’s new Stephens Family School of Medicine.

Centre Block is a mixed-use commercial project set for 10270 University Drive, a 3.5-acre site directly adjacent to the Expo Line SkyTrain’s Surrey Central Station, immediately south of Surrey City Hall and Surrey Civic Plaza.

The site was formerly home to the North Surrey Recreation Centre, which was demolished last year, and the redevelopment plans have been in the works for over half a decade now.

The project was originally planned to have four towers with heights of 43, 16, 20, and 11 storeys that would be delivered in four phases. The project has been revised several times, and the first two towers were previously set to reach 45 and 17 storeys, as previously reported by STOREYS.

The taller tower is set for the eastern half of the site (right next to the station) and the shorter tower for the western half, and the taller tower was previously planned to be delivered first. However, the shorter tower is now moving forward first, and is the focus of the development application.

Centre Block and its surrounding context. (Stantec-Revery, SCDC)

According to the development application, Phase One will now be a 12-storey building with 113,227 sq. ft of office space, 22,389 sq. ft of childcare space, 245,439 sq. ft of educational space, 48,621 sq. ft of outpatient clinic space, and 19,127 sq. ft of retail space. The building has a maximum height of 217 ft., and density of 2.9 FAR.

The ground level of the building will be shared, and be home to the retail space and a community space. SFU will then occupy Level 2 through 7, the childcare space will occupy all of Level 8, while Level 9 through 12 will be the office component.

The proposal includes 277 vehicle parking spaces and 138 bicycle parking spaces in a three-level underground parkade that will be connected to the existing City Hall parkade via P1. According to the application, SFU is requesting a 25% reduction from the minimum parking requirement, citing shared parking available at the nearby SFU Surrey Campus and Central City.

The 12-storey Phase One of Centre Block. (Stantec-Revery, SCDC)

Last October, Stantec was chosen as the architect and Stantec has since formed a joint venture with Revery Architecture. The scope of the contract includes architecture, electrical, lighting, information and communications technology, sustainability, acoustics, and building envelope design, with Stantec-Revery also to be contracted to lead the fit out of the interior space for SFU and the City of Surrey.

“The building massing is articulated as a series of vertically layered volumes that step and shift across the tower, reducing its perceived scale while creating opportunities for terraces, landscaped gardens, daylight access, and enhanced views,” said City staff in a planning report. “This approach establishes a more human-scaled profile and strengthens the project's connection to the surrounding landscape by extending outdoor amenity spaces vertically throughout the building.”

“The façade is articulated through a rhythmic, staggered pattern of vertical openings that create depth, shadow, and texture across the building envelope. Warm, natural materials reinforce the building’s architectural identity, while curved terracotta panels in a sandstoned finish wrap the volumes in a tactile and inviting expression.”

The 12-storey Phase One of Centre Block. (Stantec-Revery, SCDC)

According to the planning report, SFU’s space will include classrooms, clinical space, laboratory space, and other auxiliary space. City staff says the total capacity for the undergraduate medical school program is 360 students, and that SFU will partner with other organizations to open an outpatient clinic with physicians potentially coming from faculty members or from Surrey Memorial Hospital.

The SFU Stephens Family School of Medicine is the first new medical school in Western Canada in nearly 60 years. The program commenced in August with the first cohort of 48 students beginning classes in an interim space within SFU’s Surrey Campus. The school has a total anticipated cost of $520 million and construction is scheduled to begin before the end of 2026. The new permanent space within Centre Block is expected to be ready by Fall 2030.

RCP Consulting Ltd. was selected as the development manager, PCL Construction was selected as the construction manager, and the City of Surrey sold a 72% ownership interest in 10270 University Drive to SFU earlier this year for $34,638,808.

items.body:
Rental prices in Canada have been driven by more than just population growth. A new Bank of Canada (BoC) research paper breaks down the factors that can explain the recent surge in 1 bedroom rents from 2020 to 2026. They found that financing costs made a big contribution to higher rents, especially when rates began rising. However, the researcher still couldn’t determine what drove the initial surge at the start of 2020, before the drivers we all accept as the reason, began to appear.

Canadian Asking Rents Have Surged Over 20% Since 2021

Canadian asking rents have surged over 20% since 2021, according to the researchers. Looking at what landlords were asking for a one-bedroom apartment across a nine-city series shows a roughly 27.3% increase from Q4 2021 to Q4 2023. It’s followed by a contraction that ran until Q2 2026, but prices remain 21.0% higher than they were in Q4 2021.

As we all know, the distribution—and partial correction—varied widely by region. As BoC researcher Benjamin Straus writes, “asking rents rose sharply in nearly every major city, notably in Halifax, Québec and Calgary.”

From Q4 2021 to Q4 2023, the index shows the sharpest climbs in Calgary (+45.1%), Halifax (+32.4%), and Quebec City (+31.3%). Meanwhile, the sharp declines between Q4 2023 and Q2 2026 were led by Vancouver (-10.9%) and Toronto (-10.7%).

The surge is largely attributed to population growth, but Straus’ data reveals that was only one of the factors.

Canadian Rents Driven By Population Surge and Financing Between 2021-2024

First off, it’s important to differentiate between a factor that can explain growth statiscially and definitive cause. A tax levy doesn’t automatically flow through to rents, and X number of people don’t mean y dollars more in rent. These are estimates of what can be reasonably explained by these factors.

The analysis points to renter-household growth and financing rates as the main drivers. In 2022, the peak of the housing market and when rates began to climb, asking rents were 15.8% higher y/y in Q4. The researchers model shows household growth added 7.9 percentage points (ppts) of the growth in that period, while financing added another 7.0 ppts. This was the lion’s share of the period, with renter-households accelerating to 10.1 ppts by Q4 2023, while financing eased to 1.3 points of y/y growth. Straus writes that rising interest rates were “another key reason” for rent increases in 2022 and 2023.

Reconstructing the central bank’s index shows the growth in renter households could explain about 25 points added to asking rents from Q4 2021 to Q4 2024. The early contribution from financing slows and turns negative when rate cuts hit in 2024, adding only 5 points when all was said and done. While the analysis doesn’t touch on this point, it’s worth noting that the low rate speculative investor surge—and abrupt rate hikes that followed—amplified the influence of financing.

On the other hand, rental supply growth reduced it by 10 points. Most of that reduction likely comes from cities like Toronto and Vancouver, where the drop was attributed to a rise in the secondary rental market—i.e. the condo bubble.

Canadian Asking Rents Driven By “Unexplained Factors” Prior To Population Surge

On the note of speculative rents, the BoC model includes “unexplained factors.” In early Q1 2020, asking rents were up 6.7% y/y, with he analysis assigning 5.4 points to factors it couldn’t explain. That’s 81% of the net increase that year—before the pandemic, before rate cuts, before lockdowns.

The BoC doesn’t address this point in the research, but it stands out as it predates the surge in renter households or financing costs. It leaves a gap in the narrative, as the model identifies major contributors to the later run-up, but it can’t account for most the early growth.

That begs the question—are these factors later drivers of growth, or was a speculative bubble forming and searching for factors to support its extension?

items._ogDesc: Metro Vancouver office market weakens while industrial demand strengthens
items.body:
Vancouver’s downtown office vacancy rate climbed to 13.1 per cent in the third quarter, reaching its highest level in more than two decades as technology-sector consolidation pushed additional large blocks of space onto the market.

The increase came as the broader Metro Vancouver office market also weakened in the quarter, with overall vacancy rising 0.5 percentage point to 12.2 per cent compared with the second quarter of 2026, according to new data from CBRE Group Inc. released Thursday.

Downtown vacancy rose 0.9 percentage point during the period, while suburban vacancy edged up 0.1 percentage point.

“Two large downtown blocks of future available space were officially vacated this quarter due to consolidation within the technology sector, pushing downtown vacancy to its highest level in over 22 years,” according to the CBRE report.

“It is anticipated that these spaces will take time to absorb and hinges on reduced economic uncertainty, though recent infrastructure announcements may help spur demand more quickly.”

Vancouver’s office market has continued to lag its suburban counterpart, with the downtown vacancy rate now exceeding suburban vacancy for six consecutive quarters. Meanwhile, the gap between higher-quality and lower-quality office space narrowed during the quarter, according to CBRE.

The Vancouver market’s performance stands in contrast to improving office conditions in several other major Canadian markets.

Nationally, office markets recorded two million square feet of net absorption in the third quarter, marking the fifth consecutive quarter of positive net absorption. Nine of 11 markets tracked by CBRE recorded positive absorption, led by Toronto, Calgary and Montreal.

Industrial market shows greater resilience

While Vancouver’s office market faced pressure, Metro Vancouver’s industrial market is showing signs of strengthening.

The region’s industrial availability rate fell 0.3 percentage point quarter over quarter, while the vacancy rate remained unchanged at five per cent. Net absorption reached 1.1 million square feet in the third quarter.

“With trade disputes ongoing, we keep waiting for the other shoe to drop in the industrial market,” said Marc Meehan, research managing director of CBRE Canada, in a statement Thursday.

“Aside from some challenges in Southwestern Ontario, however, the industrial market has performed well in 2026. But in this changeable environment, the past is not prologue.”

Vancouver accounted for 10.9 per cent of new industrial construction starts nationally during the quarter behind Toronto and Montreal, according to CBRE.

The organization said both the sale and leasing markets in Metro Vancouver continue to undergo price adjustments, with many properties transacting at rates significantly below both their original asking prices from a year ago and their current marketed rates.

A total of 414,000 square feet of new supply was delivered during the quarter, nearly all of which was speculative—meaning it was built without a tenant secured in advance—bringing year-to-date deliveries to approximately 1.2 million square feet.

An additional 3.1 million square feet remains under construction, with roughly 1.1 million square feet scheduled for delivery by year-end in Metro Vancouver. Speculative developments represent about half of the space under construction, with more than 400,000 square feet expected for delivery by year-end, according to CBRE.
